Working with scam models in gratia

Source: vignettes/articles/scam-support.Rmd
scam-support.Rmd

This article shows how to plot smooths fitted with {scam}, extract estimates and intervals, sample fitted functions, and check predictions. We use increasing effects of two covariates to illustrate these operations. {gratia} also supports scam’s other one- and two-dimensional shape-constrained smooths and ordinary {mgcv} smooths fitted through scam().

We load gratia and scam before simulating the example.

library("gratia")
load_mgcv()
library("scam")

The response below combines an increasing curved effect of x and a linear effect of z, with independent Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.15. The covariates are independently sampled on the unit interval.

set.seed(46)
d <- data.frame(x = runif(200), z = runif(200))
d$y <- exp(d$x) + d$z + rnorm(nrow(d), sd = 0.15)

We fit increasing smooths for both covariates and plot their estimated contributions.

m <- scam(y ~ s(x, bs = "mpi", k = 8) + s(z, bs = "mpi", k = 8),
  data = d, not.exp = TRUE)
draw(m)

Plot smooth contributions

The captions identify the spline basis and its shape constraints. Arrows indicate increasing or decreasing effects. For a tensor product smooth, the caption identifies the constraint on each covariate. For the local constraints bs = "lmpi" and bs = "lipl", it shows the change point you specified as xc in xt. The same captions appear when drawing estimates saved with smooth_estimates(). Use smooth_type() or the .type column of the saved estimates to get a short label such as P spline (inc).

By default, draw() uses the fitted smooth’s centring, so the plotted value at a given location stays the same if you change the evaluation grid. For bivariate smooths, scam subtracts the average across the plotted grid. Use centre = "plot" to match that convention in draw() or assemble(). gratia computes the standard errors after applying the same centring. The following example fits a surface that increases with both covariates and centres it on the plotted grid.

b <- scam(y ~ s(x, z, bs = "tedmi", k = c(5, 5)), data = d,
  not.exp = TRUE)
draw(b, centre = "plot", n_2d = 40)

For univariate smooths, scam uses two standard errors for its default limits. gratia uses qnorm(0.975) for 95% normal limits. The packages can also calculate different standard errors for the same curve. gratia uses the derivative of the plotted function with respect to the fitted coefficients to calculate how their uncertainty affects the curve.

Estimate intervals, derivatives and sampled functions

For intervals and derivatives, gratia uses the covariance of the coefficients after scam applies its shape constraints. The intervals use local normal approximations, with the smoothing parameters held at their fitted values. frequentist = TRUE selects the frequentist covariance. Use overall_uncertainty = FALSE to leave out the intercept’s uncertainty. First extract pointwise smooth intervals, estimate the slope of the x smooth, and request a simultaneous band for that smooth. A simultaneous band describes uncertainty over the evaluated curve, whereas the pointwise limits apply to each location separately.

e <- smooth_estimates(m, overall_uncertainty = FALSE)
e <- add_confint(e)
head(e)

scam fits unconstrained parameters and transforms some of them to positive coefficients to enforce the smooth’s shape. Coefficient sampling draws from a normal approximation for those unconstrained parameters, then applies the same transformation. This preserves the shape constraints in every sampled curve. Because the transformation is nonlinear, the samples and the analytic intervals use different uncertainty approximations. In particular, the endpoints of an analytic interval need not satisfy the fitted shape constraint.

Use gaussian_draws() to obtain a matrix with one coefficient vector per row. Check its dimensions to confirm the number of draws and coefficients. smooth_samples() evaluates sampled smooth curves directly. We produce five draws of each smooth and plot them with draw() to see how the curves vary while retaining the fitted shape constraints.

draws <- gaussian_draws(m, n_draws = 100, seed = 54)
dim(draws)
#> [1] 100  15
samples <- smooth_samples(m, n_draws = 5, seed = 55)
head(samples)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 9
#>   .smooth .term .type          .by    .row .draw .value       x     z
#>   <chr>   <chr> <chr>          <chr> <int> <int>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 s(x)    s(x)  P spline (inc) NA        1     1 -1.00  0.00591    NA
#> 2 s(x)    s(x)  P spline (inc) NA        1     2 -0.853 0.00591    NA
#> 3 s(x)    s(x)  P spline (inc) NA        1     3 -0.749 0.00591    NA
#> 4 s(x)    s(x)  P spline (inc) NA        1     4 -0.922 0.00591    NA
#> 5 s(x)    s(x)  P spline (inc) NA        1     5 -0.898 0.00591    NA
#> 6 s(x)    s(x)  P spline (inc) NA        2     1 -0.985 0.0109     NA
draw(samples)

The .smooth column identifies the smooth, .draw identifies the coefficient draw, and .value gives the sampled function’s value at each covariate value. Fitted, derivative and response sampling functions use the same coefficient transformation. See smooth_samples() and gaussian_draws() for the returned columns and options for supplying your own coefficient draws.

Predictions and model checks

To predict the mean response as x varies, use conditional_values(). It combines both smooths and the intercept, holding z at the observed value closest to its median. The bands show uncertainty in the mean response.

predictions <- conditional_values(m, condition = "x")
predictions
#> # A tibble: 100 × 8
#>     .row       x     z .parameter .fitted    .se .lower_ci .upper_ci
#>    <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <chr>        <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#>  1     1 0.00591 0.555 mean          1.52 0.0572      1.41      1.63
#>  2     2 0.0159  0.555 mean          1.53 0.0502      1.43      1.63
#>  3     3 0.0258  0.555 mean          1.54 0.0444      1.45      1.63
#>  4     4 0.0358  0.555 mean          1.55 0.0398      1.47      1.63
#>  5     5 0.0457  0.555 mean          1.56 0.0362      1.49      1.63
#>  6     6 0.0557  0.555 mean          1.57 0.0336      1.50      1.63
#>  7     7 0.0657  0.555 mean          1.58 0.0319      1.51      1.64
#>  8     8 0.0756  0.555 mean          1.59 0.0308      1.53      1.65

#> 10    10 0.0955  0.555 mean          1.60 0.0302      1.55      1.66
#> # ℹ 90 more rows
draw(predictions)

Use appraise() to check how the model describes the observed responses. Here, quantile residuals compare each observation with its fitted Gaussian distribution. Look for departures from the reference line in the QQ plot and for changes in the spread of residuals across the linear predictor.

appraise(m, type = "quantile", seed = 56)

The model diagnostics article explains how to interpret the panels and their reference bands.

Other GAM operations

Many gratia methods for GAMs also work with scam fits, including smooth differences, response derivatives and concurvity. For custom predictions, lp_matrix() and model.matrix() return a model matrix whose columns match coef(m). When predicting with new data, gratia reuses any constants estimated when evaluating formula terms, such as means from scale(), and evaluates offsets specified in the formula. Predictions at the original observations also retain offsets supplied through the offset argument.

For supported response families with independent observations, leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO) and WAIC use the coefficient sampling approximation described above. Smoothing parameters and other fitted family parameters stay fixed. variance_comp() reports the fitted response scale divided by each smoothing parameter. These ratios describe the penalties on the coefficients before transformation.

For Gaussian identity-link fits with AR1 dependence, response simulation uses the fitted correlation and AR.start series boundaries, including observation weights. Supply the original observations so that the simulator can use their order and series boundaries. For other families, scam’s working AR1 correction alone does not define a joint response distribution. The likelihood methods for independent observations require a fit without AR1 dependence.

For GCV and UBRE fits, the covariance needed to include smoothing parameter uncertainty is unavailable. If you request model_edf(type = "unconditional") for these fits, gratia warns and returns the usual effective degrees of freedom. Confidence limits for the penalty-based variance components and MH and INLA coefficient sampling are unavailable for scam fits. To impose a supported shape restriction on an interval for a scam smooth, supply estimates and a grid directly to shape_intervals().
